Authorities: IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: $600K - sales less totally variable costs, before operating expenses

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T01: Fixed operating expenses misclassified as totally variable
ExplanationCorrect: Throughput contribution equals sales minus totally variable costs only: $1,000K - $400K = $600K. Under throughput accounting (Theory of Constraints), materials and sales commissions are the only costs that vary strictly with each unit sold; the $450K of salaries and overhead is fixed in the short run and is deducted afterward, yielding profit of $600K - $450K = $150K. The distinction drives constraint decisions: throughput of $600K measures the rate at which the system generates money before period costs, separate from the $550K gross-margin view and the $150K bottom line. Trap: treating fixed operating expenses as variable product costs and reporting $550K as throughput.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B subtracts the $450K fixed operating-expense block from sales, producing a $550K gross-margin-style residual; throughput accounting deducts only the $400K of totally variable costs, leaving $600K.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C reports $150K, which is bottom-line profit after the $450K of short-run fixed operating expenses; throughput is measured before those operating expenses, at $600K.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D restates the $450K operating expense block itself; expense levels are not a measure of money generated through sales and cannot serve as throughput.
FormulaReference: Throughput Contribution = Sales - Totally Variable Costs
Stem: From Crestline quarter: sales $1,000K, totally variable costs $400K, operating expenses $450K. Compute THROUGHPUT contribution.

Authorities: Relevant costing and expected-value decision theory
IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: Ad hoc - $16,800 beats the reservation quote
Choices.B: RESERVE the block - $15,200 expected versus $16,800 ad hoc
Choices.C: Reserve - the $8,000 fee alone decides it

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T02: Fixed retainer compared against a rival total instead of comparing totals
ExplanationCorrect: Expected overflow demand = 0.30 x 400 + 0.20 x 800 = 280 pallets. Ad hoc rental = 280 x 12 x $5 = $16,800. Reserved block = $8,000 retainer + billable usage capped at 200 expected pallets x 12 x $3 = $7,200, totaling $15,200. Because $15,200 sits below $16,800, the company should RESERVE the block and save $1,600 across the 12-month horizon. Interpretation: the retainer converts volatile spot exposure into a lower expected total cost even though some reserved capacity goes unused in low-demand states. Trap: comparing the $8,000 retainer alone against the ad hoc total instead of comparing full expected costs.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A stops at the ad hoc quote of $16,800 and never totals the reserved alternative; the reserved block costs $15,200 in expectation, so the ad hoc route is $1,600 more expensive.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C reserves but credits the decision to the $8,000 retainer alone; the retainer decides nothing by itself - the case turns on the $15,200 reserved total beating the $16,800 ad hoc total.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D abandons incremental analysis for immediate capital construction; owned-capacity economics sit outside the 12-month decision frame and were never costed, so this expected-value comparison cannot support them.
Stem: Overflow scenarios: 50 percent none, 30 percent 400 pallets, 20 percent 800 pallets. Ad hoc rental $5 per pallet-month on actual overflow; reserved 400-pallet block $8,000 per year plus $3 per pallet-month used (12-month horizon). Which option?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: ad hoc 16,800 vs reserve 15,200 -> reserve

Authorities: IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.C: Pocket price $167; realized contribution 28.1% - discount leakage removed $33 per unit

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T03: Discount waterfall halted early or computed on a shrinking base
ExplanationCorrect: Walk the discount waterfall off the $200 list price: volume discount 8% = $16; co-op advertising 5% = $10; early-payment rebate 2% = $4; freight allowance = $3. Cumulative leakage = $33, so pocket price = $200 - $33 = $167. Realized contribution = $167 - $120 = $47 per unit, which is 28.1% measured against the $200 list base ($47 / $200) - far below the 40% margin management assumed when quoting off list. Interpretation: individually small concessions compound into a $33 per-unit leak that cuts realized margin nearly in half. Trap: computing discounts on a shrinking remainder instead of on list, or halting the waterfall after the first concession.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A nets only the $16 volume discount and stops; adding the $10 co-op, the $4 rebate, and the $3 freight allowance strips another $17 and lands the pocket price at $167.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B finds the correct $167 pocket price yet repeats the assumed 40% margin; realized contribution is $47 per unit - 28.1% on the $200 list - so the assumption overstates reality badly.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D rounds the rebate and freight allowance away and reaches $170; the exact waterfall is $16 + $10 + $4 + $3 = $33 of leakage, giving $167 pocket price, $47 contribution, and 28.1% on list.
FormulaReference: Pocket Price = List Price - Cumulative Concessions
Stem: List $200; volume discount 8 percent; co-op advertising 5 percent; early-pay rebate 2 percent; freight allowance $3; variable cost $120. Pocket price and realized contribution margin percentage?

Authorities: IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.D: 1.20 - every first-pass failure consumes exactly one rework inspection

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T04: Yield ratios misapplied to process workload instead of output
ExplanationCorrect: Every started unit takes exactly one first inspection. With an 80% first-pass yield, 20% of units fail, and each of those consumes precisely one additional inspection under the single-rework policy - whether the repair later passes (75%) or scraps (25%), because scrapped units take no third test. Expected test runs per started unit = 1 + (0.20 x 1) = 1.20. The 95% ultimate yield describes good output per start, not station workload. Interpretation: quality planning must provision test capacity at 1.20 runs per started unit, 20% above nominal volume. Trap: multiplying test counts by yield ratios or extending the loop beyond the single allowed rework.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A assumes a clean first pass for every unit; with 20% failing initially and returning for a mandatory second inspection, expected runs rise to 1.20 per started unit.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B loops the 25% permanent-rework failure into an endless geometric series; policy permits exactly one rework cycle, so no unit reaches a third inspection and the added load stays at 0.20 runs.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C inflates workload with the 95% ultimate yield; yield measures successful output per start, not visits to the test station, so scaling 1.00 by yield-derived factors fabricates the 1.04 figure.
FormulaReference: Expected Runs per Unit = 1 + First-Fail Rate
Stem: First-pass yield 80 percent; failed units are reworked once - 75 percent of reworks pass permanently, the rest scrap. Expected INSPECTION RUNS per started unit?
Topic: C.189 Expected inspection runs with a rework loop

Authorities: Customer lifetime value and churn economics
IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: $1,000 - lifetime margin (40 x 25 months) caps acquisition spend
Choices.C: $600 - duration times dues ignores variable cost

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T05: Member valued on dues or single-period margin instead of lifetime contribution
ExplanationCorrect: Monthly contribution per member = $50 dues - $10 variable service cost = $40. Average membership duration = 1 / churn = 1 / 0.04 = 25 months. Lifetime margin per member = $40 x 25 = $1,000, which caps the maximum justifiable one-time acquisition cost. Steady-state breakeven membership = $60,000 fixed monthly costs / $40 = 1,500 members, so the club must hold 1,500 members to cover fixed costs, and acquisition spending beyond $1,000 per signup can never repay itself. Interpretation: retention economics, not headline dues, discipline the marketing budget. Trap: valuing a new member at a single month of margin, or at duration multiplied by dues while ignoring the $10 variable cost.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B caps acquisition at a single month of $40 contribution; the average member stays 25 months, so the recoverable stream is 25 x $40 = $1,000 and spending up to that ceiling still pays back.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C quotes $600 from a duration-times-dues shortcut that ignores the variable service cost and mis-scales the arithmetic; the correct chain is $50 - $10 = $40 monthly margin sustained for 1 / 0.04 = 25 months, a $1,000 ceiling.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D converts the churn reciprocal into a dollar figure with no margin link; 1 / 0.04 = 25 is a duration in months, and dollars require 25 x $40 = $1,000 of contribution.
FormulaReference: Customer Lifetime Value = Monthly Margin x Duration
Stem: Club: fixed monthly costs $60,000; dues $50; variable service $10; monthly churn 4 percent. Maximum one-time acquisition cost per new member that remains value-positive?

Authorities: Linear programming duality and constraint theory
IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.A: $0 - averages treat the resource as fully used rather than valuable at the margin
Choices.B: $60 PER HOUR - the contribution earned by one more unit of the binding resource, valid within a range
Choices.D: $600 - a tenfold scaling of the hourly figure

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T06: Utilization rates mistaken for marginal scarcity value
ExplanationCorrect: A shadow price is the improvement in the optimal objective value per additional unit of a binding resource. The current mix exhausts all molding hours (zero slack), and each extra molding hour converts directly into one more unit of the sole binding product carrying $60 of contribution, so the shadow price of molding capacity is $60 per hour. Every other resource holds slack, so its shadow price is $0. Linear-programming duals are local: the $60 remains valid only within a range before the optimal mix structure changes. Trap: equating high average utilization with marginal value - utilization reports how much of a resource is consumed, while a shadow price reports what one more scarce unit is worth.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A reasons from averages and assigns zero; full utilization plus a direct $60 contribution link makes molding the scarce resource whose relaxation lifts profit by $60 per hour.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C quotes the $25 shop labor rate, an input price of a non-binding resource; shadow prices attach to constraints, and shop labor carries slack here, so its own dual is $0.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D scales the answer to $600 as if ten hours moved together; a shadow price is defined per single additional unit of the resource - $60 for exactly one molding hour.
Stem: Optimal mix exhausts molding capacity (zero slack); each additional molding hour converts directly into one more unit of the sole constrained product contributing $60. Shadow price of molding capacity?
Topic: C.191 Shadow price of the binding constraint
VerifiedChecks: Independent: $60 per hour within the valid range

Authorities: Theory of Constraints scheduling (setup losses on the bottleneck)
IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.B: $320 - charging all four products a setup

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T07: Setup time on the bottleneck charged as a product cost instead of lost contribution
ExplanationCorrect: Scheduled capacity is 160 machine-hours per month. Producing four products in sequence requires three changeovers of 2 hours each, so setup absorbs 3 x 2 = 6 hours and productive run time falls to 154 hours. At $40 of contribution per run hour, effective monthly contribution = 154 x $40 = $6,160, against the naive 160 x $40 = $6,400. The changeover burden therefore costs $240 per month (6 lost hours x $40). On the constraint, every setup minute converts irrevocably into forgone contribution because those hours have no alternative use. Trap: charging setups to individual products as unit-level burdens, or counting one changeover where four product runs imply N - 1 transitions.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A prices a single changeover (2 hours x $40 = $80); a four-product schedule demands three transitions between runs, tripling the monthly loss to $240.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B bills each of the four products a 2-hour setup (4 x 2 x $40 = $320); changeovers occur between batches, and four runs create only three boundaries.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D double-counts the six setup hours, removing them from run time and again from the contribution rate; hours are either setup or run time, never both, and the loss is 6 x $40 = $240.
FormulaReference: Constraint Time Lost to Setups x Contribution per Hour
Stem: Machine 160 hours per month; four products require 3 changeovers of 2 hours each; contribution $40 per run-hour. Monthly contribution LOST to changeovers?
Topic: C.192 Changeover losses in constraint scheduling

Authorities: IMA CMA Exam Content Specification Outline - Decision Analysis

Choices.B: Reserved block - the $8,000 retainer is trivially cheap
Choices.C: Spot purchases - reservations only pay above 500 hours
Choices.D: RESERVE - $20,600 versus $23,100 at expected 420 hours; below the 320-hour indifference point spot would win

CommonTrapReference: Trap DA-T08: Crossover volume anchored to contract size instead of the cost-line intersection
ExplanationCorrect: Reserved option total = $8,000 monthly retainer + 420 used hours x $30 = $12,600, giving $20,600. Spot total = 420 x $55 = $23,100. RESERVE and save $2,500 per month at expected volume. The indifference point: each used hour saves $55 - $30 = $25, so breakeven usage = $8,000 / $25 = 320 hours; below 320 hours spot wins, above it the reservation pays. Expected usage of 420 hours clears the hurdle comfortably. Trap: comparing the retainer against the spot hourly rate instead of plotting both total-cost lines and locating the crossover volume.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A evaluates a 300-hour month, below the 320-hour indifference point where spot indeed wins; expected usage is 420 hours, where the reserved total of $20,600 beats the $23,100 spot bill.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B praises the retainer in isolation and never adds usage charges; the reservation wins because 420 saved hours x $25 ($10,500) overwhelm the $8,000 retainer, not because the retainer is small.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C anchors the crossover to the 500-hour block size; the true indifference point is $8,000 / $25 = 320 used hours, far below both the block and the expected 420 hours.
FormulaReference: Cost Indifference Point = Fixed Fee / Unit Saving
Stem: Reserved 500-hour block: $8,000 per month plus $30 per hour used; spot $55 per hour anytime; expected usage 420 hours. Reserve or spot, and cost?
VerifiedChecks: Independent: reserve 20,600 vs spot 23,100 -> reserve (indifference 320 h)
